note: Crown land is provincial or territorial. There is no single national polygon, and this map does not invent one. Non-resident rules are stricter than a U.S. BLM stay. Posted signs and the provincial atlas win.

provinces.name: British Columbia
provinces.stay: Recreation sites and informal Crown-land camping are often 14 consecutive days. Confirm the forest district.
provinces.nonResident: No single provincial camping permit for all Crown land, but some recreation sites charge a fee.

provinces.name: Alberta
provinces.stay: Public-land camping is typically 14 days where it is allowed. Public Land Use Zones have their own rules. Random camping is not legal on every acre of provincial land.
provinces.nonResident: Allowed only where public-land camping is allowed. Do not assume the Eastern Slopes are open.

provinces.name: Saskatchewan
provinces.stay: Vacant Crown land camping is commonly limited to about 21 days. Forest fringe and park land are different products.
provinces.nonResident: Confirm with the Ministry before treating a prairie section as a campsite.

provinces.name: Manitoba
provinces.stay: Crown land camping is provincial. Stay limits are often in the 21-day range and do not apply inside provincial parks the same way.
provinces.nonResident: Provincial park campgrounds are a fee. Backcountry Crown land needs the current provincial rule.

provinces.name: Ontario
provinces.stay: Crown land camping is typically up to 21 days.
provinces.nonResident: Non-residents need a Crown land camping permit. This is the province where skipping the permit is a real mistake.

provinces.name: Quebec
provinces.stay: SEPAQ parks are paid campgrounds. Public-land camping exists under provincial rules and is not a western-style BLM stay.
provinces.nonResident: Confirm the zone. Do not import a U.S. dispersed-camping habit.

provinces.name: New Brunswick
provinces.stay: Crown land camping is not the western free-for-all. Provincial parks are the straightforward option and they charge.
provinces.nonResident: Use the provincial park system unless the natural-resources office says a specific Crown site is open.

provinces.name: Nova Scotia
provinces.stay: Provincial parks and a few designated backcountry sites. Not open Crown-land camping.
provinces.nonResident: Book or follow the park rules.

provinces.name: Prince Edward Island
provinces.stay: Camp in provincial or national park campgrounds. The island is not a dispersed-camping inventory.

provinces.name: Newfoundland and Labrador
provinces.stay: Provincial parks charge. Crown-land camping rules are provincial and sparse compared with B.C.
provinces.nonResident: Confirm before you leave a highway pullout overnight.

provinces.name: Yukon
provinces.stay: Camping on territorial land is allowed outside municipalities and posted closures, with conditions. Highway campgrounds are a separate, paid system.
provinces.nonResident: Territorial land is not a reserved site. First Nations settlement land is not public camping.

provinces.name: Northwest Territories
provinces.stay: Territorial parks are the reliable overnight. Crown and territorial land outside parks is not a casual trailer base.
provinces.nonResident: Confirm with the territorial parks office.

provinces.name: Nunavut
provinces.stay: Not a drive-up dispersed system. Community and park permission matters more than a map color.
provinces.nonResident: Plan with the territorial government, not with a U.S. BLM habit.
